title: SRE SLOs, Error Budgets, Capacity Planning, Reliability Initiatives, and Runbooks
author: Ari Chen
body:
Summary:
This document consolidates Redwood Inference's SRE standards for Service Level Objectives (SLOs), error budget policy, capacity planning, reliability initiatives, incident review standards, operational tooling expectations, and canonical runbooks. It is intended for oncall SREs, service owners, platform engineers, and product managers.

Scope:
- Applies to all customer-facing inference endpoints (Redwood API: text generation, chat, embeddings, reranking), Dedicated runtime pools, and control-plane services that affect customer requests (auth, billing, routing).
- Excludes purely internal developer tools unless they affect SLAs for customer-facing services.

1) SLOs and Metrics (definition and targets)
Overview:
- SLOs are expressed as availability (success rate) and latency percentiles for each product surface. Every service must publish a primary SLO and one or two secondary SLOs.
Primary SLOs (examples):
| Service         | Primary SLO (Availability) | Secondary SLO (Latency)                 | Measurement Window |
|-----------------|----------------------------|------------------------------------------|--------------------|
| Redwood API (gen) | 99.95% successful responses (5xx & client-fatal excluded) | p95 < 350 ms end-to-end token latency | 30 days           |
| Embeddings API  | 99.99% successful responses  | p99 < 450 ms                            | 30 days           |
| Dedicated Inference | 99.9% job-ready capacity (within SLA) | median < 200 ms scheduling latency | 30 days           |
| Control Plane (auth/routing) | 99.99% API success | p95 < 100 ms                          | 30 days           |

Metric definitions and ownership:
- "Successful response": HTTP 2xx or 3xx for customer requests; for streaming endpoints, a session is successful if the final completion is delivered without server-side error.
- Latency windows measured from request ingress to first-byte (for streaming: time-to-first-token) and to final-token for batch jobs.
- Service owners must publish the SLI query, dashboard link, and collection method in the service README. Example SLI queries are stored in the monitoring repo under /slis/*.

2) Error Budgets and Burn Policy
Error budget calculation:
- Error Budget = (1 - SLO) * Window. Example: For 99.95% over 30 days, error budget = 0.05% of requests.
- Error budget is tracked in absolute failed requests and percentage.
Burn policy (standard):
- Green (safe): < 25% of monthly error budget used. Normal ops.
- Yellow (watch): 25% - 50% used. Owner notified; reduce risky rollouts; suspend nonessential changes that touch serving path.
- Orange (restricted): 50% - 90% used. Pause all releases to affected services; require canary/feature-flag gating; hold product-facing promotions.
- Red (exhausted): > 90% used or budget exhausted. Emergency controls: rollback recent changes, restore last known-good model/variant, scale capacity, and invoke incident bridge.
Procedures when burn thresholds crossed:
1. Pager duty: Alert channel and service owner notified within 15 minutes (automated).
2. Triage call (30 minutes): Review recent deployments, traffic changes, model rollouts, and infra events.
3. Mitigation plan (60 minutes): Identify short-term mitigations (rollback, increase capacity, route to fallback model).
4. Postmortem requirement: Any incident that causes >10% of monthly budget to be consumed or crosses Orange/Red requires a blameless postmortem (see section 6).

3) Capacity Planning and Headroom
Goals:
- Maintain 20% usable headroom at quart-hour granularity for customer-facing pools; 99th percentile peak planning should allow for 2x observed hourly burst during major events.
- Dedicated pools contracted via reserved capacity should maintain contractual throughput + 15% headroom for transient spikes.
Capacity signals and runbooks:
- Key signals: GPU utilization, queue length, tail latencies (p95/p99), model warm cache hit rate, scheduling latency, and instance startup time.
- Scaling rules: Autoscaler scales when queue length per-worker > 50 requests or average GPU utilization > 72% for 3 consecutive minutes. Downscale after 10 minutes of sustained utilization < 40%.
- Capacity review cadence: Quarterly capacity refresh with telemetry review and yearly forecasting tied to sales commitments. Responsible: Capacity Planning team (eng-sre) + Platform Product.
Planning artifacts (required):
- Traffic forecast (CSV link)
- Service capacity runbook (dashboard links, SLI, cost per token estimates)
- Model warmup plan and cache sizing numbers

4) Reliability Initiatives and Roadmap Alignment
Principles:
- Prioritize work that reduces risk to primary SLOs per unit developer effort. Prefer automation (self-healing), observability, and fast rollback paths.
Operational initiatives (examples):
- KV/prefix cache improvements to reduce p95 latency by 20% for hot prompts (Q2 2026).
- Continuous canary gating for model rollouts with automated quality gates (A/B evaluation + traffic ramp) (Q3 2026).
- Model-fallback library: standardized routing to quantized/lightweight variants when high latency/error observed (Q4 2026).
KPIs to track for initiatives:
- SLO attainment rate across services, mean time to mitigation (MTTM), change-failure-rate (CFR), and reduction in manual intervention steps.

5) Incident Review and Postmortem Standards
When to write a postmortem:
- Any Sev1 outage impacting customer-facing 99% of users for >5 minutes, or any time orange/red error budget thresholds are crossed.
Required postmortem structure (minimum):
- Title, Sev level, detection time, mitigation time, recovery time, owners, incident timeline (minute-level), root cause, contributing factors, impact (requests, customers affected), remediation plan with owners and deadlines, and follow-up verification steps.
Blamelessness and timeline:
- Postmortem should be drafted within 48 hours and published (internal) within 7 days. A blameless review meeting with stakeholders should be scheduled within 14 days.
Severity classification guidance:
- Sev1: Complete service disruption causing >= 5 minutes of degraded service for >= 10% of paying customers.
- Sev2: Partial degradation causing elevated latencies or error rates impacting critical flows.
- Sev3: Minor degradation or non-customer-facing incidents.

6) Operational Tooling and Dashboards
Minimum dashboard set for each service:
- SLO dashboard (availability + latency with rolling window),
- Error budget burn rate and historical trend,
- Top 10 error types and traced transactions,
- Capacity dashboard (GPU/CPU utilization, queue lengths, instance counts),
- Recent deploys and canary metrics.
Tooling standards:
- Alerts must be actionable and tied to runbook steps; avoid noisy alerts. Alert thresholds should map to SLO burn stages when possible.
- Tracing: All request paths must include a trace id propagated through services. Sampling: 100% for errors, 5% for success by default.
- Runbook links must be discoverable from each dashboard's top-right corner and the incident page.

7) SRE Runbooks (canonical examples)
Runbook: High error-rate (API errors > 0.5% sustained for 5m)
- Pager triggers: alert to #oncall-sre and service-owner channel.
- Step 1: Acknowledge alert and capture incident channel (Bridge link).
- Step 2: Check recent deploys: `git log --since="2 hours" --oneline` and deployment dashboard. If deployment in last 60m, rollback or pause rollout.
- Step 3: Check model changes: model id, quantization profile, and recent model weights. If new model, route 50% traffic to last-known-good variant.
- Step 4: Scale up capacity by 20% (if autoscaler not sufficient) using `kubectl scale` or autoscaler override (documented in runbook).
- Step 5: If error type indicates infrastructure (e.g., OOM, GPU driver), open infra incident and escalate to infra-systems owner.
- Step 6: Once mitigated, monitor for 30 minutes before closing bridge. Draft postmortem if >10% monthly budget consumed.

Runbook: High latency (p95 > 250ms for 5m)
- Step 1: Confirm SLI dashboard and identify whether latency is ingress, model execution, or network.
- Step 2: If model execution: verify KV cache hit rate and GPU utilization; if cold-cache or high GPU util, scale or route to lighter variant.
- Step 3: If scheduling delay: inspect queue length and autoscaler status; trigger manual scale if needed.
- Step 4: If degraded downstream (e.g., control plane), route traffic to fallback region or degrade nonessential features (tracing sampling, debug logging).

Runbook: Capacity exhaustion for Dedicated pools
- Step 1: Notify account ops and engineering leads.
- Step 2: Temporarily increase burst capacity if policy allows and notify customer.
- Step 3: If burst capacity unavailable, prioritize requests based on tiering policy and route lower-tier traffic to BestEffort queue.
- Step 4: Initiate provisioning workflow for new capacity (owner: gpu-fleet-and-capacity).

8) Ownership, Escalation, and Communication
- Service Owner responsibilities: maintain SLI/SLO definitions, own runbooks, review error-budget burn weekly, and sign off on major rollouts.
- Oncall SRE responsibilities: first-responder triage, runbook execution, and incident bridge management.
- Escalation matrix: 0-15m: Oncall -> 15-60m: Service Owner -> 60m+: Engineering Manager/Director. For infra/hardware incidents escalate to GPU Fleet oncall immediately.
- Customer communication: For Sev1 affecting customers, Customer Success drafts status updates within 30 minutes and posts to status.redwood.ai; engineering provides technical summary within 2 hours.

9) Verification and Compliance
- All remediation actions tied to postmortem must include verification steps and owners. Verification evidence (logs, restored metrics) must be attached to the postmortem.
- Quarterly audit: eng-sre will validate that each service has an up-to-date runbook and SLO dashboard.

Appendix A: Example Alert Thresholds (suggested)
- API 5xx rate > 0.5% for 5m -> Sev2 alert.
- API 5xx rate > 2.0% for 3m or any 5xx spike affecting >10% of customers -> Sev1.
- p95 latency > 250ms for 10m -> Sev2.
- Error budget burn rate > 100% over 1 day -> Page to oncall + owner.

Appendix B: Useful CLI snippets
- Check recent deploys: `kubectl get deploy -o wide --selector=service=<svc>`
- Scale deployment: `kubectl scale deployment/<deploy> --replicas=<n>`
- Route to fallback model (example): `redwoodctl route set --service <svc> --model <model-id> --weight 0.5`

References and links:
- Monitoring repo: git@repo:redwood/monitoring (SLI queries and dashboard templates)
- Incident review template: /confluence/eng-sre/incident-review-template
- Capacity planning template: /confluence/eng-sre/capacity-planning-template

Document maintenance:
- Review cadence: eng-sre will review and update this document quarterly or after any Sev1 incident.
- Contact: eng-sre (oncall rotation) and capacity-planning@redwood.ai for questions.
